# The Macro Trap

In SAS, macros are text substitution. They are powerful but hard to debug.
In R, you write **Functions**. Functions are first-class citizens. They accept objects as input and return objects.

## Writing a Simple Function

SAS Macro:
```sas
%macro print_stats(dset, var);
  proc means data=&dset;
    var &var;
  run;
%mend;
```

R Function:
```r
print_stats <- function(df, col_name) {
  df %>%
    summarise(
      mean_val = mean(.data[[col_name]], na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_val = sd(.data[[col_name]], na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

print_stats(dm, "AGE")
```

*Note: The `.data[[col_name]]` syntax is needed for "Tidy Evaluation" when passing column names as strings.*

# Iteration: The `purrr` Package

Stop writing `%DO` loops. Use `purrr` to `map` a function over a list of inputs.

## Map: Apply function to each element

Suppose you have a list of files to read.

```r
library(purrr)
library(readr)

files <- c("data/cohort1.csv", "data/cohort2.csv", "data/cohort3.csv")

# Read all files into a list of dataframes
data_list <- map(files, read_csv)

# Read all files and stack them immediately into one dataframe
all_data <- map_dfr(files, read_csv)
```

## Iterating over Columns

Calculate mean for every numeric column.

```r
dm %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  map(mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Control Flow

R has standard if/else and for-loops, but you rarely need loops for data manipulation.

```r
# Standard If
if (nrow(dm) > 0) {
  print("Data exists")
}

# For loop (use sparingly)
for (i in 1:10) {
  print(i)
}
```
